entities.summary:
Ye Shi, courtesy name Zhengze (正则), pseudonym Mr. Shuixin (水心先生), was a Chinese neo-Confucian of the Song dynasty.

Born in the late 12th century, Ye Shi's philosophical writings, primarily in the neo-Confucian tradition, significantly influenced the intellectual landscape of late imperial China.

His most notable works include the 'Zhengze Lun' (正则论) and the 'Shuixin Ji' (水心记), which examined the human condition, ethics, and the nature of reality.

Ye Shi's ideas were shaped by the tumultuous politics and social upheaval of the Song dynasty, yet his thoughts continued to inspire subsequent generations of Confucian scholars.

In the 13th century, his teachings were disseminated throughout the empire by the influential Confucian scholar, Zhu Xi, cementing Ye Shi's legacy in the annals of Chinese philosophy.

The enduring relevance of Ye Shi's ideas can be seen in the continued study and application of neo-Confucian thought in East Asian cultures.

The impact of Ye Shi's philosophical contributions can be seen in the works of prominent Chinese thinkers, such as Wang Yangming and Yu Xuanji, who built upon his ideas.

In the 20th century, Ye Shi's writings were rediscovered and reinterpreted by scholars, who recognized the significance of his neo-Confucian philosophy in the context of modern Chinese thought.

Today, Ye Shi is recognized as a major figure in the history of Chinese philosophy, whose ideas continue to inspire scholars and thinkers around the world.

Ye Shi's philosophy remains a vital part of China's cultural heritage, offering insights into the human condition, ethics, and the pursuit of wisdom.

In the context of the Song dynasty, Ye Shi's significance can be seen in his ability to navigate the complexities of imperial politics and social change, while remaining true to the core principles of Confucianism.

Ye Shi's legacy extends beyond China's borders, influencing the development of East Asian thought and culture.
